transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess I'm here because... it really all started when my in-laws moved into our house. Which, you know, we have a decent-sized place—it’s a four-bedroom colonial we bought a few years ago—but suddenly it feels like a shoebox. They brought this massive antique dining set that completely blocks the hallway, and my father-in-law is always, always watching the Golf Channel. I mean, who watches golf for six hours straight on a Tuesday? 

But anyway... because of all that, I’ve just been so keyed up and completely worn down. It's like I have zero fuse left. I’m snapping at my wife constantly over the smallest things. And it's bleeding into my work. I'm a manager for musicians, and lately, I'm just avoiding calls I would normally handle immediately. I'll just sit at my desk and watch the phone ring. I actually... I nearly let a major contract for one of my guys completely fall apart because I just couldn't think straight. The venue promoter was trying to mess with the merchandise split—usually we do an 80/20 split, but they were pushing for 70/30, which is ridiculous for a weekend show—and normally I'd be all over them, but I just couldn't focus to save my life.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even before your in-laws moved in?

No, no, not at all. Before they backed that U-Haul into my driveway, things were actually really good. I wasn't down or... whatever you said. Actually, my wife and I had just gotten back from Cabo a few weeks prior. We stayed at this all-inclusive place, which I usually avoid because, you know, the drinks are always completely watered down. They use that cheap well tequila that just gives you a massive migraine the next day. 

But this place? They had top-shelf everything. I ended up talking to the bartender—great guy, Mateo—for like two hours about agave harvesting. Did you know it takes like seven to ten years for a blue agave plant to mature before they can even make tequila out of it? Seven years! Imagine putting all that work in and just waiting. It’s actually a lot like breaking a new indie band, honestly. You book them in these tiny, gross clubs in Brooklyn for years, hauling amps through the slush, just hoping one A&R guy from a decent label actually shows up and pays attention... 

Wait, what was the question again? Oh, right, feeling hopeless. No, I was completely fine before they moved in. Really.
In the time since your in-laws moved in, have there been days when you felt down or really struggled to get through the day, not just stressed or overwhelmed?

I mean... down? I don't know about down. I'm just so wound up and exhausted from dealing with them. It's not like I'm sitting around crying, you know? I'm just... I'm drained. Like, I walk in the door and my mother-in-law is immediately asking me if I want a cup of tea. Which sounds nice, right? But she doesn't just make tea. She has this whole ritual with this loose-leaf stuff she orders from some specialty shop in London. It's ridiculous. And she uses this tiny little strainer that she insists has to be washed by hand, immediately, with this specific unscented soap, otherwise it "ruins the patina" or whatever. 

I actually tried to buy her a normal box of Earl Grey once—just standard, off-the-shelf stuff from Whole Foods, nothing crazy—and she looked at me like I had handed her a cup of dirt. It's just exhausting. You try to do something nice, or at least normal, and it turns into a whole production. Kind of like dealing with lead singers, honestly. You get them a perfectly good green room with a decent deli tray, and they throw a fit because the M&Ms aren't separated by color. I had this one guy in Austin... man, he completely trashed a dressing room because the sparkling water wasn't Pellegrino. 

But yeah, I wouldn't say I'm hopeless or anything. Just... really, really stressed out.
